invasive.title: Virginia invasive plant signage law (Code of Virginia § 3.2-3801.1)
invasive.edition: Code of Virginia § 3.2-3801.1 (2025, cc. 393, 409), effective January 1, 2027, as printed by the General Assembly's Legislative Information System on 2026-10-31

jurisdictions.notes: The rule prints "Oplismenus hirtellus spp. undulatifolius" (wavyleaf basketgrass): "spp." is read as subspecies and written "subsp.", since the list format has no place for the misprinted rank. All three tiers carry the same duty: "The movement of a regulated article is prohibited unless accompanied by a valid certificate or permit" (2VAC5-317-30), where "move" means to ship, offer for shipment, receive for transportation, carry, or otherwise transport, move, or allow to be moved. The rule says nothing of selling, planting or propagating as such; the statute requires a permit before selling or offering for sale a noxious weed into or within the state where the Board requires one (§ 3.2-804), and the Board's rule requires one for movement. Tiered as bans because moving the plant within the state is forbidden without a permit; permits are for movement to a specified destination under limited handling, use, processing or treatment, or for experimental or scientific purposes (2VAC5-317-40). Tiers 1 and 2 differ from Tier 3 only in that the Commissioner may eradicate or suppress them, by destruction, seizure, stop sale, stop delivery, treatment or return to origin (2VAC5-317-80). The statute's definition of "move" (§ 3.2-800) excepts "bona fide agricultural purposes including the management, tilling, planting, or harvesting of agricultural products"; the rule's own definition doesn't repeat the exception. Phase-out: § 3.2-802 A, updated in 2026 (2026, c. 66), gives any plant commercially propagated in Virginia a phase-out "upon being designated as a noxious weed" of two years for grasses, forbs and vines, four for shrubs and seven for trees. The rule names no plant as being phased out, and the statute doesn't say whether this reaches plants listed before 2026. The 2024 additions (Trapa bispinosa to Tier 2; Alliaria petiolata through Ulmus pumila to Tier 3, effective July 4, 2024) were proposed when the statute's definition of noxious weed still excluded plants commercially propagated in Virginia (quoted in the Virginia Register, Vol. 40, Iss. 2, 2023). Phragmites australis and Pueraria montana are listed as species, with no subspecies or variety excepted. The invasive class (§ 3.2-3801.1) takes effect January 1, 2027, and until then has no force. It is tiered listed: selling stays legal with the signs, which must identify the plant as invasive, educate consumers about invasive plant species and encourage them to ask about alternatives; without them the Commissioner must issue a stop-sale order until the signs are posted. It names botanical names only. Kew's accepted names, checked in its checklist (2026-10-31): Egeria densa, Ficaria verna, Mahonia bealei, Oshuna crassipes and Securigera varia are homotypic synonyms of Elodea densa, Ranunculus ficaria, Berberis bealei, Pontederia crassipes (water hyacinth) and Coronilla varia; Cenchrus purpurascens Thunb. is a heterotypic synonym of Cenchrus alopecuroides (Chinese fountain grass, sold as Pennisetum alopecuroides), and is matched as that species. Kew makes Trapa bispinosa a variety of Trapa natans, and Ampelopsis brevipedunculata a variety of Ampelopsis glandulosa, so both are matched by their printed names only (a listed species would take in the whole species, and the other varieties are not listed). Left out: the Department of Conservation and Recreation's invasive plant list (§ 10.1-104.6:2), which the law has DCR create and which binds only state agencies (no agency may plant, sell or propagate its plants), the list itself not being printed in law; and the tradesperson-notice rule § 3.2-802 C calls for, proposed as 2VAC5-455 in February 2025 and not in the Administrative Code as of 2026-10-31. Also left out: the box tree moth quarantine (2VAC5-332, effective March 11, 2026), which needs a certificate or permit to move Buxus from Clarke and Frederick Counties and the City of Winchester to unregulated areas, a pest quarantine on a host plant in named places, not statewide; and, not read, the seed law (2VAC5-390) and the endangered plant rule (2VAC5-320), which protects plants rather than restricting them.

jurisdictions.title: Georgia live plant rules: federal noxious weeds (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 40-4-9-.07)
jurisdictions.edition: Rules of the Georgia Department of Agriculture, Rules 40-4-9-.07 and 40-4-9-.11 as amended effective October 13, 2010, in the Secretary of State's compilation current through rules filed through October 22, 2026; the plants are 7 CFR 360.200's, Code of Federal Regulations revised as of January 1, 2025

classes.federal: Federal noxious weed in Georgia: its sale or distribution in the state is prohibited (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 40-4-9-.07)

jurisdictions.notes: The rule names no plant of its own. It prohibits "The sale or distribution of any plant listed on the Federal Noxious Weed list or determined by the Commissioner to be a public nuisance" (40-4-9-.07(1); also an unlawful act, 40-4-9-.11(b)), and a Federal Noxious Weed is "Any plant listed under Title 7, Code of Federal Regulations, Part 360" (40-4-9-.01(h)). So this list adopts the US entry's plants (7 CFR 360.200), by reference, as the rule does: it names no edition, so it changes whenever the federal list does. No plant "determined by the Commissioner to be a public nuisance" was found: the rules name none, and their former subject "Declaration of Public Nuisance" (40-4-22) was repealed effective October 16, 2013. The rule forbids sale and distribution; it says nothing of a plant already growing on someone's land. Out-of-state growers and dealers may sell live plants into Georgia only if they "are not designated as a Federal Noxious Weed" (40-4-9-.04(1)(a)). Breaking the chapter is a misdemeanor (40-4-9-.12(4)). The Secretary of State's robots.txt closes the single-rule pages to crawlers; the text was read from the subject page and the history from the Department 40 PDF, both on the same official site and both allowed. Left out: the seed rule (40-12-4-.01), with its own noxious weed seed list; and the pest and disease quarantines, which certify host plants rather than restrict them as weeds: vegetable transplants entering Georgia (40-4-7), phony peach (40-4-13), blueberry scorch virus (Vaccinium, 40-4-24) and citrus (Citrus and related genera, and Murraya, 40-4-26). Not read: the statute (O.C.G.A. Title 2, Chapter 7), whose official online text is published through LexisNexis's web application; the rule cites O.C.G.A. §§ 2-7-1 et seq. and 2-7-14 as its authority and sets the effect itself.

jurisdictions.notes: The statute lists the first noxious weeds (§1519); the Controlled Plant and Noxious Weed Committee adds plants by notice in the Pennsylvania Bulletin, effective 60 days after publication (§1511(b)(3)(iv)). The full lists are read from the Department of Agriculture's list page: the Bulletin notices, and any sales phase-in they set, could not be read, as pacodeandbulletin.gov's robots.txt shuts out all but named crawlers. Neither saved department page gives a phase-in date. Every plant §1519 names is on the department's page. Hydrilla verticillata, Class A in §1519(a), is Class B on the department's page, and is shown as B (same effect). Wavyleaf basketgrass: the department prints Oplismenus hirtellus; it is recorded narrower, as the statute prints it, "Oplismenus hirtellus (L.) P. Beauv. Subsp. undulatifolius" (§1519(a)(9)). Japanese blood grass: the department lists "Imperata cylindrica 'Red Baron'" in Class A, a cultivar the list format can't name; it isn't recorded there, since the whole species is on the federal list, which makes it a Class C noxious weed here, under the same ban. Class C is every federal noxious weed not established in Pennsylvania and not otherwise listed (§1519(c)); §1502 makes every federal noxious weed a noxious weed here. So this list adopts the US entry's plants into Class C, by reference (the department's page: "includes the Federal Noxious Weed list by default as Class C weeds"); Stratiotes aloides, which the department names, is recorded as well. A plant on both lists takes its Pennsylvania class first. Left out: "Cuscuta spp., except for native species" and "Orobanche spp., except for native species", since the rule names neither the natives it spares nor the others (the federally listed dodders and broomrapes are in the US entry); Nitellopsis obtusa (starry stonewort), an alga; "Sorghum bicolor L. Moench (commonly known as shattercane)", which names no weedy form and read whole would make grain sorghum a noxious weed; "Pastinaca sativa (except for non-wild cultivated varieties)", wild parsnip, which a species name can't tell from the garden parsnip the rule excepts. Lythrum: "Exotic Lythrum species, including Lythrum salicaria L. (commonly known as purple loosestrife), the Lythrum salicaria complex and Lythrum virgatum L. (commonly known as European wand loosestrife), their cultivars and any combination thereof": the two named species are recorded. Amaranthus rudis and A. tuberculatus are printed as two entries. Printed with synonyms, recorded by the first name: Tripidium ravennae [Saccharum ravennae, Erianthus ravennae]; Cynanchum louiseae/Vincetoxicum nigrum; Cynanchum rossicum/Vincetoxicum rossicum; Rhamnus frangula [Frangula alnus]; Persicaria perfoliata ("formerly known as Polygonum perfoliatum L."). Exempted cultivars, on the department's exempted-varieties page (https://www.pa.gov/en/agencies/pda/plants-land-water/plant-industry/noxious-weeds-and-controlled-plants/exempted-varieties-information-application.html, read 2026-10-31), named in the line for each of the three species, since the list format names no cultivar: Japanese barberry, the WorryFree series Crimson Cutie (UCONNBTCP4N), Lemon Cutie (UCONNBTB113), Lemon Glow (UCONNBTB048) and Mr. Green Genes (UCONNBTB039), and Proven Winners Sunjoy Todo and Sunjoy Mini-Maroon; glossy buckthorn, Rhamnus 'Fine Line'; European privet, 'Golden Ticket'. The statute itself has no section on exempting cultivars. Permits: a noxious weed may be cultivated and propagated only under an individual permit for research and educational purposes (§1512(a)(1)); controlled plants under a general or individual permit (§§1512 to 1514). Hemp is listed as a controlled plant on the department's page; the committee's notice and Pennsylvania's hemp chapter were not read. Not read: 7 Pa. Code Ch. 110 (pacodeandbulletin.gov's robots.txt); the law it was made under, the Noxious Weed Control Law of 1982, was repealed by Act 46 of 2017, §3(2). Seed law (7 Pa. Code Ch. 111, which §1511(c) points weed seeds to) is left out. Kew's accepted names, checked in its checklist (2026-10-31): Cynanchum louiseae, Cynanchum rossicum, Egeria densa, Ficaria verna and Rhamnus frangula are homotypic synonyms of Vincetoxicum nigrum, Vincetoxicum rossicum, Elodea densa, Ranunculus ficaria and Frangula alnus; Amaranthus rudis and Humulus japonicus are heterotypic synonyms of Amaranthus tuberculatus and Humulus scandens (Japanese hops), and are matched as those species. Kew makes Pueraria lobata a variety (Pueraria montana var. lobata) and Lonicera standishii part of Lonicera fragrantissima subsp. fragrantissima, so both are matched by their printed names only.

jurisdictions.title: Kentucky noxious weeds and invasive plants on state rights-of-way (KRS 176.051; 603 KAR 3:100)
jurisdictions.edition: 603 KAR 3:100 effective January 25, 2022 (48 Ky.R. 1434, 2075); KRS 176.051 as amended 2017, effective June 29, 2017 (Kentucky Legislative Research Commission)

classes.rightofway: Noxious weed or invasive plant under Kentucky law: the state Department of Highways must keep state rights-of-way free of it (KRS 176.051; 603 KAR 3:100)

jurisdictions.notes: No Kentucky law found bans selling or planting a named plant. The one plant list beyond seed law is KRS 176.051(1), as 603 KAR 3:100 amends it: it binds the Department of Highways on state rights-of-way (and its help to abutting owners who ask), not landowners, nurseries or gardeners. Only three entries print a botanical name: Sorghum halepense, Cirsium arvense and Carduus nutans. Left out, common names only: multiflora rose, kudzu, poison hemlock, marestail, Amur honeysuckle, Japanese knotweed and common teasel (KRS 176.051(1)), and spotted knapweed and cutleaf teasel (added by 603 KAR 3:100, Section 1(1)); "marestail" could mean more than one plant. Giant foxtail, a common name only, was deleted by 603 KAR 3:100, Section 1(2). Checked and left out: the seed law's noxious weed seed list (12 KAR 1:120, limits on weed seed in agricultural seed); KRS Chapter 249, whose thistle laws (KRS 249.180 to 249.195: landholders to cut Canada thistles, thistle eradication areas) were repealed by 2022 Ky. Acts ch. 131, effective July 14, 2022, and whose remaining noxious weed sections (KRS 249.420, 249.430) let the Department of Agriculture run control programs and issue regulations but name no plant; 302 KAR (Department of Agriculture), which has no noxious weed or invasive plant regulation; KRS 249.040 quarantines, which are against plants carrying insect pests or plant diseases and name no plant; 301 KAR 1:122 (Fish and Wildlife), which bars buying, selling or releasing "any aquatic species not native or established in Kentucky waters" (aquarium use excepted) but names only animals, so gives no plant list. 2025 House Bill 640, to let the Energy and Environment Cabinet regulate invasive non-native plants, did not pass (last action March 12, 2025: to the Senate's Committee on Committees).

jurisdictions.notes: The Administrative Code itself (the Office of Administrative Hearings' site, reports.oah.state.nc.us) could not be read: it is served only over http, and its https port does not answer from here. So 02 NCAC 48A .1702 and .1703 are read in the North Carolina Register's printing of the rules as approved (26:09, November 1, 2011). OAH's periodic review report for 02 NCAC 48A (submitted January 22, 2019) still gives October 1, 2011 as the last amendment of both rules, and the Department of Agriculture's current noxious weed list names the same plants; an amendment after 2019 could not be ruled out without the Code. Not read, for the same reason: .1701 (definitions), .1704 (regulated articles), .1705 and .1706 (the certificates and limited permits that are the rule's only exception), .1707 and .1708. Class A item (1) is "All weeds listed in 7 C.F.R. 360.200 which is hereby incorporated by reference including subsequent amendments and editions": so this list adopts the US entry's plants into Class A, by reference; its own entries come first. "Salvinia spp. (all except S. minima)" is the genus, with Salvinia minima excepted (the rule abbreviates the genus). The rule prints "Trappa spp." (water-chestnut): entered as the genus Trapa, which the Environmental Quality rule prints, since a genus entry carries no Kew spelling. Read narrower than printed: Class B's "Lythrum – Any Lythrum species not native to North Carolina", which names no species, as purple loosestrife, Lythrum salicaria, which 15A NCAC 02G .0602 names and the Department of Agriculture's list calls this entry ("Purple loosestrife (Lythrum spp. not native to NC)"); other non-native Lythrum are covered by the rule but not entered, because a genus entry would take in North Carolina's native Lythrum species, which the rule excepts without naming them. Class C: "regulated area" is read as the counties .1703(a)(14) names for Oriental bittersweet (the rule's heading is "Regulated Areas"; .1701, which may define it, was not read); inside those counties the rule does not forbid selling it, but forbids moving it out; tiered ban because it forbids moving it into the state. Class B and C plants each have named counties they may not be moved from (.1703(a)(1)-(3), (6)-(14)). Violating these rules is a Class 3 misdemeanor (G.S. 106-423.1). Noxious aquatic weeds: the Department of Environmental Quality designates them (G.S. 113A-222); the statute lets the Secretary control them in the state's waters (G.S. 113A-223) and lets the Commissioner of Agriculture regulate their sale as plant pests under the plant pest law (G.S. 113A-224), and neither the statute nor .0602 forbids selling or growing them, so tiered listed; the section's other rule, 15A NCAC 02G .0601, was not read. Left out of the aquatic class: the 16 species printed under "Species Listed on the Federal Noxious Weed List" that are still on it (shown by the federal entry, and Class A by .1702(a)(1)); and Crassula helmsii, Lagarosiphon spp., Ludwigia hexapetala, Lythrum salicaria, Myriophyllum spicatum, Salvinia spp. ("All except S. rotundifolia") and Trapa spp., which are on 02 NCAC 48A and shown there. Stratiotes aloides is printed under the federal heading but is no longer a federal noxious weed: entered here. Phragmites australis is printed as the whole species, the native American subspecies too. The Environmental Quality copy of .0602 names the Department of Environment and Natural Resources and may differ from the codified text. Not included: the seed rules (02 NCAC 48C), the witchweed quarantine (02 NCAC 48A .0500, not read; Striga is on the federal list), and advisory lists. jurisdictions.notes: Read 2026-10-31 under Jason's exception for official legal-code sites (codes.ohio.gov's robots.txt turns away all automated readers): only the pages named, with the honest user agent, at least 6 seconds apart; every request answered 200. Phase-in, OAC 901:5-30-01(C): the ban did not apply to Pyrus calleryana until January 7, 2023, or to Ligustrum vulgare until January 1, 2026; both dates have passed. The rule was first effective January 7, 2018; this version took effect February 13, 2023. Exceptions in the same rule: reed canary grass sold for use as animal feed (C)(3); disposing of a listed plant, controlling it, or using it for research or education under a department compliance agreement, in a way that does not spread it (D). The director may exempt a cultivar if scientific evidence shows it is not invasive (F); the rule names none. Purple loosestrife: ORC 927.682 forbids selling, offering for sale or planting Lythrum salicaria plants or seed without the director's permit; permits may be issued for controlled experiments, and the director must by rule exempt any variety shown not to threaten the environment. I found no such exemption rule. It is on the invasive list too, whose line (the same ban, and more) is the one shown; a plant on two lines takes the first. Multiflora rose: ORC 927.681 forbids selling, offering for sale or planting "any variety of multiflora rose plants or seed" without a permit, except that a licensed nurseryman may plant it as rootstock for other roses. The statute gives only the common name, so it adds no entry; Rosa multiflora is on the invasive list. Despite the name, OAC 901:5-37-01 and ORC 5579 do not forbid selling or planting a "prohibited noxious weed": the duties are to cut or destroy it on the township's notice (ORC 5579.05, 5579.06) and along roads (5579.04, 5579.08), so that class is listed. The noxious class is read from https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-901:5-37-01 (effective February 16, 2025) and https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-5579. Left out of the noxious class: grapevines (Vitis spp.), listed only "when growing in groups of one hundred or more and not pruned, sprayed, cultivated, or otherwise maintained for two consecutive years"; a whole-genus entry would mark every garden grape. Also left out: Phyllostachys aureasculata (yellow groove bamboo), listed only "when the plant has spread from its original premise of planting and is not being maintained", which a planted, kept bamboo isn't; and Sorghum bicolor ("shatter cane", in both the rule and ORC 5579.04(A)) and Pastinaca sativa ("wild parsnip"), whose common names mean the weedy forms, so read whole they would take in grain sorghum and the garden parsnip. Salsola kali var. tenuifolia is the statute's own Russian thistle (ORC 5579.04(A)); the rule lists Russian thistle as Salsola tragus. Both are entered. ORC 5579.05 also reaches "wild parsnip, wild carrot, oxeye daisy, wild mustard, or other harmful weeds"; wild carrot, oxeye daisy and wild mustard are common names only and add no entries. Misspellings as printed: "Hesperis matronlis" and "Marsilea guadrifolia" (OAC 901:5-30-01); "Persicaria perfoliate" (OAC 901:5-37-01). Written in the catalog's form: "ssp." (OAC 901:5-30-01) and "sub." ("Lepidium draba sub. draba", OAC 901:5-37-01) as "subsp."; "Typha x glauca" and "Sorghum x almum" with the × sign. ORC 901.50 authorizes the invasive plant rule, OAC 901:5-30-02 creates its advisory committee, and ORC 927.51 holds nursery-stock definitions; none of them lists plants. Not included: Ohio's seed-law noxious weed seed lists, and pest quarantines or plant-pest orders under ORC 927.70 and 927.71, which were not read. Kew's accepted names, checked in its checklist (2026-10-31): Calystegia sepium, Conyza canadensis, Egeria densa, Eichhornia azurea, Fallopia japonica, Ficaria verna, Monochoria hastata and M. vaginalis, and Senecio glabellus Poir. (cressleaf groundsel; not the later homonym of S.Y.Hu) are homotypic synonyms of Convolvulus sepium, Erigeron canadensis, Elodea densa, Pontederia azurea, Reynoutria japonica, Ranunculus ficaria, Pontederia hastata and P. vaginalis, and Packera glabella. Kew writes crack willow as a hybrid, Salix × fragilis, and "Salix fragilis" only as a misapplied name, so it is matched by its printed name only. Hedge bindweed carries the background note it has on the Arkansas and Texas lists.

jurisdictions.notes: Since P.A. 103-620 (eff. 1-1-25) the Act names no plants: Section 3 leaves the list to the Department of Natural Resources' rules, and the list is 17 Ill. Adm. Code 1100.30. The rule says: "Name of plant species vary for the same species and can change. Updates of nomenclature do not remove the exotic weed designation of a species." Phase-in: callery pear, Pyrus calleryana, is listed "starting January 1, 2028": until then it is listed, not banned; from that date its class should become exotic, tier ban. Permits (1100.40) are only to sell or distribute non-viable material, or to plant viable material to study control in a controlled environment or as biological control in the wild. The Act exempts commercial propagation of exotic weeds for sale outside Illinois, certified under the Insect Pest and Plant Disease Act (525 ILCS 10/4(b)). Violations are a Class B misdemeanor, and exotic weeds offered for sale may be confiscated and destroyed (525 ILCS 10/5); a municipality may order them eradicated on all property within its limits (10/4(d)). The rule exempts no varieties. Dipsacus spp. and Tamarix spp. are entered as genera; the rule prints "Reynoutria x bohemica", entered with the × sign. Noxious weeds: 505 ILCS 100 and Part 220 set a duty to control and eradicate them (505 ILCS 100/3; 220.10), and forbid moving articles infested with them, nursery stock and sod included, until cleaned (220.230); they do not forbid selling or planting the plants, so listed. Giant ragweed and common ragweed are noxious only "within the corporate limits of cities, villages, and incorporated towns": class noxiousTown; both are native. Marihuana, Cannabis sativa: the Act's definition of noxious weed "does not include industrial hemp as defined and authorized under the Industrial Hemp Act" (505 ILCS 100/2). Read narrower than printed: "Perennial members of the sorghum genus, including johnsongrass (Sorghum halepense), sorghum almum, and other johnsongrass X sorghum crosses with rhizomes" as Sorghum halepense and Sorghum × almum (printed "sorghum almum"); the genus is not entered, since its annual members (grain sorghum) are not listed, and the unnamed "johnsongrass X sorghum crosses with rhizomes" are left out. blackCurrant.title: West Virginia white pine blister rust quarantine on black currant (W. Va. Code §19-12-6)
blackCurrant.edition: Department of Agriculture's White Pine Blister Rust Quarantine, established October 19, 1967, amended May 11, 1992; W. Va. Code chapter 19, article 12 (Plant Pest Act), as published on code.wvlegislature.gov, printed November 1, 2026 (UTC)

jurisdictions.notes: Read 2026-10-31. The Secretary of State publishes 61CSR14A as a scanned PDF of the final filing (filed April 13, 2023, effective May 1, 2023, authorized by SB 361, passed March 11, 2023; sunset August 1, 2033). Its text was read from the Word file of the same filing on the same page, and checked against the scan: section 5 by eye, Appendix A by OCR (the same names). The rule declares the plants; the statutes say what may not be done with them. W. Va. Code §19-12-14 (Plant Pest Act): no person may sell, barter, expose, offer for sale, or move, transport, deliver, ship or offer for shipment into or within the state any noxious weed in any living stage without a federal permit, where applicable, or a state permit, which may be issued only if it is not injurious, is generally present already, or is for scientific purposes under safeguards; read at https://code.wvlegislature.gov/pdf/19-12/. §19-12D-7(b) (Noxious Weed Act) likewise forbids moving it into or within the state without a permit. Violations are misdemeanors (§19-12-16; §19-12D-11). Japanese barberry (§5.2): the Commissioner may exempt cultivated varieties found sterile and of no threat to agriculture; neither the rule nor the Department of Agriculture's in-state nursery page names any exempted cultivar. The Department's news release of June 2, 2020 said its sale became illegal on July 1, 2020, after a phase-in for existing stock under the 2018 rule (not read); the 2023 rule has no phase-in, so the ban is in force. Multiflora rose: declared a noxious weed by statute (§19-12D-5(b)); §19-12D-12 makes importing, bringing or moving it into the state, or selling, offering or exposing it for sale, or possessing it with intent to sell, a misdemeanor, and forbids the Commissioner to grant any permit for its sale or its movement into the state. The Department's in-state nursery page says garden roses grafted or budded onto multiflora rootstock may be shipped into the state; the statute names no such exception. Federal list: §5.4 adopts the Federal Noxious Weed List as an extension of the state list and prints it as Appendix A, 'as of November 10, 2010'. It is entered as printed (class federal), not by reference to the US entry, because it is a dated list whose names differ from the current CFR's in places: Digitaria scalarum, Mimosa invisa and Homeria spp. are printed, and Cuscuta jepsonii, C. nevadensis and C. occidentalis are among the excepted dodders. The Cuscuta exceptions are entered as printed; five are misspelled ('ceanothii', 'cephalanthii', 'corylii', 'exalta', 'vetchii'), and their correct spellings, as the US entry has them, are in exceptAlso. Left out: Caulerpa taxifolia, an alga. 'Avena sterilis Linnaeus (including Avena ludoviciana Durieu)': both entered, as in the US entry. Sagittaria sagittifolia is printed twice: entered once. 'Rubus fruticosus Linnaeus (complex)': entered as the one species. Printed with capitals, entered lower-case: 'L. Morrowii' (Lonicera morrowii), 'Inula Britannica', 'Onopordum Illyricum'. Abbreviated genera written out: 'C. crispus' and 'C. nutans' (Carduus), 'P. cuspidatum' (Polygonum), 'L. Morrowii' (Lonicera). Misspelled, with the correct spelling in kew: 'Elaeagnus umbellate', 'Lonicera tartarica', 'Carthamus oxyacantha' (as the US entry has it), 'Setaria pallide-fusca' (hyphen dropped). For the reviewer, names Kew files under other accepted names: Polygonum cuspidatum, Polygonum perfoliatum, Pueraria thunbergiana (kudzu; Kew: Pueraria montana var. lobata), and in the appendix the names the US entry reviewed. Narcotic plants: §19-12D-8(c) lets the Commissioner help destroy 'marijuana or hemp, Cannabis spp., or other plants which produce drugs which have been condemned for destruction under the narcotics laws' and says 'Such drug producing plants are hereby declared noxious'; rule §5.3 is 'reserved for narcotic drug producing plants' and names none. Read as reaching only plants condemned under the narcotics laws, so there is no Cannabis or Papaver entry; the Department's nursery page lists marijuana ('Canabis sativa') and opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) among noxious weeds, but no statute or rule read names the opium poppy, and hemp is licensed under the Industrial Hemp rule (61CSR29, not read). Quarantines: orders of the Commissioner under W. Va. Code §19-12-6, which 61CSR14 §2.14 names ('White Pine Blister Rust Quarantine, Black Stem Rust Quarantine') and whose violation its Table 61-14-A fines; read from the Department's PDFs, https://agriculture.wv.gov/wp-content/uploads/WV_Black_Stem_Rust_Quarantine.pdf (May 11, 1992) and https://agriculture.wv.gov/wp-content/uploads/WV_Blister_Rust_Quarantine.pdf (1967, amended May 11, 1992). Black stem rust: all species and varieties of Berberis, Mahonia and Mahoberberis are considered rust-susceptible, and prohibited, except those the USDA designates rust-resistant or immune (§§IV, VI); the quarantine names none, so the three genera are entered whole with no exceptions, though the USDA's list (not read) exempts many species and cultivars: the class line states the exception, but a 'every Berberis species' line would overstate it. Japanese barberry is entered first as a noxious weed and takes that line. Blister rust: European black currant (Ribes nigrum) may not be moved to any destination in the state (§II), entered before the genus. Every other currant and gooseberry (Ribes, natives included): 'dissemination, growing or other uses' are prohibited only in the 23 counties the quarantine names (§I), where the Commissioner may destroy them (cultivated species other than European black currant only within 1,500 feet of white pine stands, §III); tiered listed because the ban does not reach the rest of the state and the app cannot tell counties apart, though inside those counties it is a ban. Not law, left out: the seed law and its noxious weed seed list (61CSR9; W. Va. Code chapter 19, article 16) and advisory lists. Checked, no plant list: 61CSR14 (Plant Pest Act rule), the active rules of the Division of Natural Resources (title 58), and the gypsy moth quarantine (an insect pest). Reviewer (2026-10-31): left out, as other states' host-plant quarantines are: the Barberry and Black Stem Rust Quarantine, whose ban on every Berberis, Mahonia and Mahoberberis excepts those the USDA designates rust-resistant without naming them (genus entries would cover the resistant barberries and mahonias most gardens have); and the blister rust quarantine's ban on every Ribes in 23 named counties (county-limited, as Virginia's box tree moth quarantine). Kept: the same quarantine's statewide ban on moving European black currant. Kew's accepted names (2026-10-31): the appendix's federal names as the US entry records them, checked there; and Polygonum cuspidatum and Polygonum perfoliatum, Kew's Reynoutria japonica (heterotypic) and Persicaria perfoliata (homotypic). Pueraria thunbergiana and Setaria pallidefusca, which Kew makes a variety and a subspecies (Pueraria montana var. lobata, Setaria pumila subsp. pallidefusca), are matched by their printed names only.

jurisdictions.notes: Noxious weeds (Department of Agriculture and Industries, 80-10-14): the rule prohibits "The movement of Class A, B, or C noxious weeds or any regulated article infested with Class A, B, or C noxious weeds into or within Alabama", "Except as permitted in 80-10-14-.07 and 80-10-14-.08" (80-10-14-.05(1)). It does not mention sale or planting; all three classes are tiered ban because it forbids moving the plants into or within the state. Permit exceptions: scientific permits "to allow the movement of noxious weeds in any living stage and any regulated articles for scientific purposes" (.08(3)); limited permits for "noncertified regulated articles" (a regulated article includes "Any noxious weed", .02(13)) to specified destinations for limited handling, utilization, processing or treatment when the inspector finds no hazard of spread (.08(2)); and the nursery rule's special permits for the entrance of "noxious weeds that are needed for experimental purposes" (80-10-1-.11(2)). Certificates (.08(1)) are for articles found free of noxious weeds. Inspectors may seize, treat or dispose of articles moving in violation (.10); "Evidence of noxious weed shall be considered a public nuisance" (.02(12)); violations carry the penalties of Code of Ala. 1975, §2-25-22 (.12). Class A item (a) is "All weeds listed in 7 C.F.R. 360.200 Federal Noxious Weed List, the same of which is hereby incorporated by reference herein including its subsequent amendments and editions" (also .13): so this list adopts the US entry's plants into Class A, by reference; its own entries come first. Printed misspellings, with Kew's spelling given: "Althernanthera philoxeroides", "Potamgeton crispus", "Eichornia crassipes", "Stratlotes aloides". Fatoua villosa is printed with the common names "Hairy crabgrass, mulberry weed": entered by its botanical name. Phragmites australis is printed as the whole species, the native American subspecies too. Nonindigenous aquatic plants (Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, 220-2-.124, amended effective October 15, 2026; text in chapter 220-2, https://admincode.legislature.state.al.us/api/chapter/220-2): the rule lists the plants "which are prohibited by Section 9-20-3 from being introduced or placed or caused to be introduced or placed into public waters of the state". It forbids nothing else (selling, growing or moving them, or planting outside public waters), so listed. The Alabama Nonindigenous Aquatic Plant Control Act itself (Code of Ala. 1975, §§9-20-1 to 9-20-7) was not read: its only official online text is the Legislature's browser application; the class sentence is worded from the rule. Penalty: §9-20-6. Left out of the aquatic class: Lyngbya wollei (a cyanobacterium, not a plant); 11 printed plants that are also in 80-10-14's classes, where they show as banned (Alternanthera philoxeroides, printed "Alternanthera philoxeriodes"; Egeria densa; Potamogeton crispus; Myriophyllum spicatum; Eichhornia crassipes; Myriophyllum aquaticum; Lythrum salicaria; Najas minor; Stratiotes aloides; Pistia stratiotes; Trapa natans); and 6 that are federal noxious weeds, so Class A in Alabama by reference and shown by the federal entry (Salvinia molesta, Hydrilla verticillata, Hygrophila polysperma, Limnophila sessiliflora, Eichhornia azurea, Ipomoea aquatica, printed "Ipomea aquatica"). "Lagarosiphon spp" is entered as the genus; its one federal species, Lagarosiphon major, is also Class A by reference. Nymphoides cristata is printed "(synonym N. hydrophylla)". Left out: the seed rules (80-11), with their own noxious weed seed lists; the nursery rules (80-10-1), which name no plants; the pest and disease quarantines on host plants (80-10-4, -5, -7, -10, -15, -19, -20), not read; and the boll weevil rule that non-commercial cotton "shall not be planted in an elimination area without a waiver" (80-10-12-.11(3)), since the rule that set out the elimination area (80-10-12-.05) was repealed effective 9/24/07. Advisory lists (for example the Alabama Invasive Plant Council's) are not law. Not read: the Alabama Plant Pest Act (Code of Ala. 1975, Title 2, Chapter 25), the authority for 80-10-14 (§2-25-4), whose official online text is the same browser application. Kew's accepted names (2026-10-31): Egeria densa, Eichornia crassipes (Eichhornia), Landoltia punctata and Polygonum perfoliatum are homotypic synonyms of Elodea densa, Pontederia crassipes, Spirodela punctata and Persicaria perfoliata; Polygonum cuspidatum, Ludwigia uruguayensis and Nymphoides cristata are heterotypic synonyms of Reynoutria japonica, Ludwigia grandiflora and Nymphoides hydrophyllum, and are matched as those species.

jurisdictions.notes: Part 413 lets the Commission of Agriculture and Rural Development add or delete plant species by order (MCL 324.41302(1)). The Commission's Invasive Species Order Amendment No. 1 of 2026 (effective May 20, 2026; read from the copy Jason saved from michigan.gov, which refuses automated readers: https://www.michigan.gov/mdard/-/media/Project/Websites/mdard/documents/boards/agcommission/2026-Invasive-Species-Order.pdf) adds water hyacinth, printed "Water-hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes)", and water lettuce (Pistia stratiotes) to the prohibited species, "30 days after this order is signed", so from June 19, 2026; and Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii), glossy buckthorn (Frangula alnus), Callery pear (Pyrus calleryana) and common buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica) to the restricted species: "sale and cultivation of these species will be allowed in 2026 and 2027. Restriction of these species begins January 1, 2028" (class restricted2028, listed until then; on that date they move to restricted, a ban). The order excepts no cultivars. It amends a standing Invasive Species Order, which with any earlier amendments (a 2015 order on water soldier, Stratiotes aloides, is reported) was not read and may list more plants. The statute's lists are entered as printed. Each listed plant includes "a hybrid or genetically engineered variant of the species" and, for terrestrial plants, "a fragment, including a seed or other propagule" (324.41301(1)(k), (o)): the species are recorded; the hybrids are not entered (so Bohemian knotweed, a Japanese knotweed hybrid, is covered by the statute but not matched). Prohibited and restricted plants carry the same duties; they differ in the fines (324.41309) and in one exception: an aquatic restricted species may be possessed as a department order under 324.41302(6) allows for naturalized organisms. Possession does not include plants merely present on one's land unless one knowingly introduced them, plants kept only where they were found in the wild, or plants held to be promptly destroyed (324.41301(2)). "Introduce" is to "stock, place, plant, release, or allow the release" at a location "where the organism is not already naturalized" (324.41301(1)(f)); permits to introduce a plant are the Department of Agriculture and Rural Development's (324.41305(b)). Purple loosestrife: "cultivars of purple loosestrife developed and recognized to be sterile and approved by the director of the department of agriculture and rural development under section 16a of the insect pest and plant disease act, 1931 PA 189, MCL 286.216a, are not a restricted species"; MCL 286.216a and the list of approved cultivars were not read. Japanese knotweed is printed "Fallopia japonica" and listed as prohibited. Phragmites: printed "Phragmites or common reed (Phragmites australis)" with no exception for the native subspecies (americanus), though a restricted species must be "not native" (324.41302(3)(b)); recorded as printed: the reviewer should decide whether to narrow it. Giant salvinia is printed "Salvinia molesta, auriculata, biloba, or herzogii": four entries. Left out of the prohibited list: cylindro (Cylindrospermopsis raciborskii), a cyanobacterium, and starry stonewort (Nitellopsis obtusa), an alga; and the non-plant species. Noxious weeds (1941 PA 359): the landowner's duty is to destroy them; the act forbids no sale or planting, so listed. It does not apply to weeds in small-grain fields (247.64(4)); a county, city, township or village may add "any other plant" it regards as a common nuisance (247.62(1)(l)), not entered; "Noxious weeds does not include milkweed (any species of the genus Asclepias)" (247.62(2)). Read narrower than printed: "Mustards (charlock, black mustard, and Indian mustard, species of the genus Brassica or Sinapis)" as charlock, Sinapis arvensis; black mustard, Brassica nigra; and Indian mustard, Brassica juncea (the mustard-greens crop); the genera are not entered, which would take in cabbage and its kin. Recorded as printed, for the reviewer: "Wild carrot (Daucus carota)": the species includes the garden carrot, which the act does not except; "Ragweed (Ambrosia elatior L.)", entered without the author. Dodders: "any species of the genus Cuscuta", natives included. Natives on the noxious list: the native dodders, common ragweed, poison ivy and poison sumac. Giant hogweed is on both lists: shown as prohibited. Left out: the seed law's noxious weed seed lists (1965 PA 329), the departments' watch list and other advisory lists, and pest quarantines on host plants. Reviewer (2026-10-31): left out of the noxious weeds: "Mustards (charlock, black mustard, and Indian mustard, species of the genus Brassica or Sinapis)", whose species are named by common name only (the genera would take in cabbage and its kin); and "Wild carrot (Daucus carota)", whose species takes in the garden carrot, as Ohio's and Pennsylvania's wild parsnip and shattercane are left out. Kew's accepted names (2026-10-31): Fallopia japonica, Eichhornia azurea, Eichhornia crassipes, Egeria densa, Monochoria hastata and M. vaginalis, Polygonum perfoliatum and Salvinia herzogii as Reynoutria japonica, Pontederia azurea, Pontederia crassipes, Elodea densa, Pontederia hastata and P. vaginalis, Persicaria perfoliata and Salvinia biloba; Ambrosia elatior, a heterotypic synonym of Ambrosia artemisiifolia, is matched as that species.

jurisdictions.notes: Invasive Species Management Act, P.L.2025, c.290, approved January 20, 2026, "This act shall take effect immediately" (§11). Its own list (§4a, N.J.S.A. 23:2A-20) names 30 plants; item (31) adds any species the Department of Environmental Protection lists by rule, and none has been adopted: the Act gives it 12 months (§7a), and the Department of Agriculture's page shows its rule, N.J.A.C. 2:19-3, as "(Coming Soon)". Phase-in: propagating, importing or otherwise introducing a listed plant is forbidden "Commencing on the first day of the 13th month next following the effective date" (§4b), counted here as February 1, 2027; selling, distributing, exporting or offering it or its seeds, from "the first day of the 49th month" (§4c), counted as February 1, 2030. The Department of Agriculture's page gives January 1, 2027 and January 1, 2030. Neither date has come on 2026-10-31, so the class is listed; from the first of these dates its tier should become ban. §4c begins "except as provided under P.L.1963, c.29 (C.4:8-17.13 et seq.)", a law not read. §4d applies the bans to "any non-hybrid sub-species, variety, cultivar, or other subcategory" of a species listed by rule. Waivers: a conditional use waiver is "an authorization issued by the Department of Environmental Protection that provides for a limited, specified use of a prohibited invasive species" (§3); its process is to be set by rule (§7a), and the Department of Agriculture's concurrence is sought for agricultural waivers. The Department of Agriculture enforces first for selling, offering, propagating for sale or importing; civil administrative penalties are $1,000 to $2,000 (§9). The Act supersedes contrary local ordinances (§8). Exempt cultivars (§4e), which must be labelled and sold with the Invasive Species Council's educational materials: Berberis thunbergii Aurea, UCONNBTCP4N, UCONNBTB113, UCONNBTB048 and UCONNBTB039; Miscanthus sinensis NCMS1 and Tift M77. The exemptions "shall expire two years after the effective date of this act" (January 20, 2028) unless continued by rule (§4f). Entries can't except cultivars, so the species are recorded whole. "running bamboo (Phyllostachys)" is entered as the genus; the Department of Agriculture's page prints "Phyllostachys species". That page also misprints "Humulus japonicas", "Lespedeza cuneate" and the porcelain berry as a subspecies; the statute's names are used. jurisdictions.notes: Plant pests: S.C. Code Regs. 27-135 names no plants. It says "The official listing of plant pests in SC shall be maintained and made publicly available on Clemson's website" (27-135(3)), and the Department of Plant Industry's list page says "This page shall serve as the official listing of plant pests in accordance with South Carolina Code of Regulations Chapter 27 Article 10". The page is undated; it was read on October 31, 2026, and only its plant table is entered (the rest lists insects, diseases and other pests). What the law prints: the Director may "determine and implement appropriate measures to eradicate, control, or slow the spread of plant pests" (27-135(1)); a nursery's inspection "must reveal that ... the Nursery Stock is sufficiently free from Plant Pests" (27-161(B), 27-162(B)); plants entering the state "found infested with Plant Pests shall be declared a public nuisance" (27-163(D)(2)); and the Commission may "seize, quarantine, treat, or otherwise dispose of the plant pest, host, or article" (S.C. Code §46-9-60(A)) and stop the sale of plant material sold or grown in violation (§46-33-100). Neither the regulation, the statutes read, nor the list page says a listed plant may not be sold, planted or moved, so by the law's own words the class would be listed. The Department of Plant Industry says otherwise: its news release of July 14, 2021 (not law) says "Typically, when a species is added to the State Plant Pest List, the change goes into effect immediately and it becomes illegal to move or sell it that same day", and that the listing of Pyrus calleryana, Elaeagnus umbellata, Elaeagnus angustifolia and Elaeagnus pungens "will make them illegal to sell or trade within South Carolina" but "it will not be illegal to possess them", with "The ban on sales" beginning October 1, 2024 (a date already past) and covering "Bradford pear trees and any other pear trees grown on the commonly used Pyrus calleryana rootstock". The South Carolina Noxious Weed Act (S.C. Code §§46-23-10 to -90) lets the Director designate noxious weeds and the Commission seize or quarantine those new to or not widely prevalent in the state; its one prohibition is on moving a noxious weed out of a county the Commission has quarantined for it (§46-23-40(c)). No separate noxious weed list and no such county quarantine were found. Entered as printed, with authors dropped ("(Mart.) Griscb.", "R. Brown", "H.B.K.", "Trin."). "Avena sterilis, A. ludoviciana" is two entries. "Indula brittanica" is printed for Inula britannica. The Orobanche exceptions are printed with the genus abbreviated ("O. bulbosa" ...) and two misspelled, "O. fasciculate" and "O. uniflorum": entered as printed, with the federal list's spellings, Orobanche fasciculata and Orobanche uniflora, as exceptAlso. Left out: Caulerpa taxifolia, an alga; and "Cuscuta spp.", printed "Dodders, with some exceptions" without naming them (the federal entry shows Cuscuta with its exceptions). Read as printed: Phragmites australis, the whole species, native American subspecies too. Prohibited aquatic plants: S.C. Code §50-13-1415 says "No person shall possess, sell, offer for sale, import, bring, or cause to be brought or imported into this State, or release or place into any waters of this State any of the following plants: (1) Water Hyacinth (2) Hydrilla Provided, however, that the department may issue special import permits to qualified persons for research purposes only." "Hydrilla" is entered as the genus Hydrilla, the printed word. "Water Hyacinth" is a common name only and is not entered; Eichhornia crassipes, which the plant pest list calls "Water hyacinth", shows in the pest class. The section lets the department add species by regulation; none was found in the Department of Natural Resources' regulations (chapter 123). The Department of Environmental Services' "illegal aquatic plants" page and flyer are not law and were not used. Not entered, because the rules name the plants by common name only (for the reviewer to decide): currant and gooseberry plants, which "No person, firm, or corporation shall knowingly plant ... within any such Blister Rust Control Area unless a special permit shall have been issued", nor move there from elsewhere in the state, and which may be destroyed there as a public nuisance (27-11); Clemson's regulated-areas page puts Spartanburg, Greenville, Pickens and Oconee counties in the area. And cotton: "Non-commercial or ornamental cotton shall not be planted without the prior written approval of the Director" (27-1096(C)), and "ornamental cottonseed" and "individual potted specimens of cotton plants" are "prohibited from sale or distribution within the state" (27-1099(B)). Left out: the witchweed quarantine (27-40 to 27-50; Striga is on the plant pest list and the federal list), which requires a certificate or permit to move it out of the regulated area, Horry and Marion counties; the other pest and disease rules on host plants (tomato and tobacco transplants, 27-20, 27-30; Asian longhorned beetle, 27-58; sweetpotato weevil, 27-60 ff.; plum pox virus, 27-75, which bars planting Prunus for a year after eradication in a quarantined area, none at present; light brown apple moth, Phytophthora ramorum and citrus greening, 27-77 to 27-79; phony peach, 27-80; Japanese beetle, 27-100 ff.; imported fire ant, 27-120 ff.; Asian citrus psyllid, 27-137; seed Irish potatoes and sweet potatoes, 27-140, 27-150); seed certification and seed rules with noxious weed seed limits; and advisory lists. The Legislature's Code of Regulations is unannotated and says it "is not official"; it is current through State Register Volume 50, Issue 3 (effective March 27, 2026). Violations: misdemeanor (S.C. Code §46-9-90(A); §46-23-80). Reviewer (2026-10-31): tiered ban by the agency's reading, Jason's decision (2026-10-31: "Flag them red, and say something along the lines of 'by agency reading'"). No regulation or statute read says a listed plant may not be sold; Clemson University's news release of July 14, 2021 (saved: sc-clemson-news-194130) says "Typically, when a species is added to the State Plant Pest List, the change goes into effect immediately and it becomes illegal to move or sell it that same day", that the ban on selling Callery pear (and pears grown on its rootstock) and three Elaeagnus began October 1, 2024, and that keeping plants already owned stays legal. Left out: Oryza sativa (printed "Red Rice and Asian rice") and Citrus reticulata var. unshu (Satsuma), crops whose listing the list doesn't explain; read whole they'd mark rice and satsumas as banned, as Ohio's shattercane and wild parsnip are left out. Kew's accepted names (2026-10-31), by which these are also matched: Calonyction muricatum as Ipomoea muricata; Centaurea repens as Rhaponticum repens; Cnicus benedictus as Centaurea benedicta; Egeria densa as Elodea densa; Eichhornia azurea as Pontederia azurea; Eichhornia crassipes as Pontederia crassipes; Emex australis as Rumex hypogaeus; Emex spinosa as Rumex spinosus; Euphorbia prunifolia as Euphorbia heterophylla; Ficaria verna as Ranunculus ficaria; Indula brittanica as Pentanema britannica; Leptochloa chinensis as Dinebra chinensis; Ludwigia uruguayensis as Ludwigia grandiflora; Monochoria hastata as Pontederia hastata; Monochoria vaginalis as Pontederia vaginalis; Nymphoides cristata as Nymphoides hydrophyllum; Pennisetum clandestinum as Cenchrus clandestinus; Pennisetum macrourum as Cenchrus caudatus; Pennisetum pedicellatum as Cenchrus pedicellatus; Polygonum perfoliatum as Persicaria perfoliata; Prosopis alpataco as Neltuma alpataco; Prosopis argentina as Neltuma argentina; Salsola vermiculata as Caroxylon vermiculatum; Salvinia herzogii as Salvinia biloba. Euphorbia prunifolia is a heterotypic synonym of Euphorbia heterophylla in Kew's checklist, and is matched as that species. Matched only as printed (Kew gives no one accepted species for them, or a broader one): Avena ludoviciana, Pennisetum polystachion, Setaria pallide-fusca.

jurisdictions.notes: Read from the rule's sections as Jason saved them from the Department of State's NYCRR on govt.westlaw.com on 2026-10-31: 575.1 to 575.6 and 575.8 to 575.11, and 192.1. The pages are headed "OFFICIAL COMPILATION OF CODES, RULES AND REGULATIONS OF THE STATE OF NEW YORK", in a window titled "Unofficial New York Codes, Rules and Regulations". Part 575 is "Current through November 15, 2024" and 192.1 "Current through February 28, 2022". The pages print no history notes. The Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) gives Part 575's effective date as March 10, 2015. Not saved: 575.7 (petitions to add or remove species) and 575.12 (severability). Phase-in, past: 575.3(f) let Japanese barberry be possessed, sold, purchased, transported or introduced "for a maximum of one year following the effective date of this Part"; DEC dates the end March 9, 2016. Prohibited plants "shall only be disposed of in a manner that renders them nonliving and nonviable" (575.3(e)). Permits: a prohibited species may be possessed with intent to sell, import, purchase, transport or introduce it under a DEC permit "for research, education, or other approved activity" (575.9(a)). A regulated species may be introduced into a free-living state only under a permit "expressly authorizing such introduction" (575.9(b)). Exemptions, 575.8(a). The Part does not apply to: (1) incidental or unknowing possession, sale and the like, not due to a failure to take reasonable precautions; (2) possession or transport to control or manage an existing infestation; (3) possession or transport for identification or disposal; (4) a cultivar of a listed species that DEC determines reproduces mainly sexually and does not revert to its parent's invasive traits. Such a cultivar must be completely sterile or have no reproductive parts, or demographic modeling must predict it can't establish expanding populations in natural areas. "the department will publish a list of cultivars meeting the criteria of this subparagraph in the State Register and Environmental Notice Bulletin. Only cultivars listed pursuant to this section are eligible for this exemption". The rule itself names no cultivar. DEC's Environmental Notice Bulletin of November 16, 2022 lists nine as "Conditionally Exempt": Berberis thunbergii 'Aurea', 'UCONNBTCP4N' (Crimson Cutie), 'UCONNBTB113' (Lemon Cutie), 'UCONNBTB048' (Lemon Glow) and 'UCONNBTB039' (Mr. Green Genes); Miscanthus sinensis 'NCMS1' (My Fair Maiden) and 'Tift M77' (Scout); Euonymus fortunei 'Kewensis' and 'Vanilla Frosting'. Entries can't except cultivars, so the species are recorded whole, and Japanese barberry's line (prohibitedBarberry) names its five, as Pennsylvania's does; (5) holders of a DEC or Agriculture and Markets permit for disposal, control, research or education; (6) work under a compliance agreement, limited permit or certificate of inspection; (7) permitted biological control agents; (8) wetland plants in a wastewater vegetation treatment unit permitted before the Part was adopted. Regulated species: they "shall be legal to possess, sell, buy, propagate and transport" (575.4(b)). The duties are in 575.6. A sale label or written notice, "Invasive Species-Harmful to the Environment" in at least 14-point bold type, must offer non-invasive alternatives and care instructions. A landscaper must give the customer written notice before supplying or planting one. Buyers must follow and keep the instructions. A free-living state is defined in 575.2(m). It means public lands and waters, lands and waters connected to them, natural areas, and water-using facilities whose outflows give direct access to public waters. For fish and aquatic plants it excludes artificial ponds with no outlet to public waters and private waters not connected to public waters. Agriculture and Markets inspects registered growers and dealers for compliance (575.11). Printed as whole species, and entered so: Phragmites australis (lv), with no exception for the native subspecies; Oplismenus hirtellus (lii), the species, not subspecies undulatifolius; Myriophyllum heterophyllum (xlviii), the species itself, besides the hybrid (xlix). Misspelled: "Hydrocharis morus-ranae" (xxx), entered as printed with Kew's spelling. Left out: (xlix) "Myriophyllum heterophyllum x M. laxum", a hybrid printed by its parents. Printed with synonyms in parentheses, recorded by the first name: Centaurea stoebe (C. biebersteinii, C. diffusa, C. maculosa misapplied, C. xpsammogena), so diffuse knapweed, C. diffusa, appears only as a synonym and is not entered; Cirsium arvense (C. setosum, C. incanum, Serratula arvensis); Cynanchum louiseae (C. nigrum, Vincetoxicum nigrum); Cynanchum rossicum (C. medium, Vincetoxicum medium, V. rossicum); Dioscorea polystachya (D. batatas); Ficaria verna (Ranunculus ficaria); Frangula alnus (Rhamnus frangula); Imperata cylindrica (I. arundinacea, Lagurus cylindricus); Ludwigia hexapetala (L. grandiflora); Persicaria perfoliata (Polygonum perfoliatum); Reynoutria japonica (Fallopia japonica, Polygonum cuspidatum); Reynoutria sachalinensis (Fallopia sachalinensis, Polygonum sachalinensis); "Reynoutria x bohemica (Fallopia x bohemica, Polygonum x bohemica)". "Lonicera x bella" and "Reynoutria x bohemica" are entered with the × sign. Black currant, 6 NYCRR 192.1 (https://govt.westlaw.com/nycrr/Document/I21ef9955c22211ddb7c8fb397c5bd26b): the ban holds statewide, except for cultivars "immune or resistant to white pine blister rust disease or currant rust (Cronartium ribicola) as described in section 192.2" and "in designated fruiting currant districts as defined in section 192.3". 192.2 and 192.3 were not saved, so the resistant cultivars and the districts are not named here. Left out: 192.4, white pine blister rust quarantine districts, which in an unofficial copy bars every Ribes from named counties and towns only; it was not saved, and covers named districts only. Also left out: seed-law lists and advisory lists. Kew's accepted names (2026-10-31), by which these are also matched: Achyranthes japonica as Achyranthes bidentata; Cynanchum louiseae as Vincetoxicum nigrum; Cynanchum rossicum as Vincetoxicum rossicum; Egeria densa as Elodea densa; Ficaria verna as Ranunculus ficaria; Humulus japonicus as Humulus scandens. Matched only as printed (Kew gives no one accepted species for them, or a broader one): Ampelopsis brevipedunculata.

jurisdictions.notes: The list is the Department of Agricultural Resources' Massachusetts Prohibited Plant List as of May 2026, read from the copy Jason saved from mass.gov (www.mass.gov refuses automated readers), with the Department's decisions of December 8, 2025 and May 11, 2026. What the list forbids, from the list page (saved by Jason, November 1, 2026): "Following is a list of plants, including all cultivars, varieties and hybrids, for which the sale, import, trade, purchase, distribution, propagation, and related activities are currently prohibited within the state of Massachusetts". The page names no one it binds. Of newly added plants, the page says "nursery agents/growers may no longer receive or begin propagation of those species. Existing stock is subject to the following phase-out periods, determined by growth form (1 year for herbaceous plants, 2 years for shrubs, 3 years for trees)", and the two decisions that "Agents/Growers will no longer be able to receive new stock, or begin growing new stock, but may sell any existing stock during the phase-out period". Legal basis: neither the list nor the decisions names the law it is made under. Each decision follows a public hearing and written comments, and finds that the plants "pose a threat to land in Massachusetts". M.G.L. c. 128, §27 lets the director, after a public hearing, prohibit the delivery into the Commonwealth of plants likely to carry pests or disease, and make rules to carry out §§16 to 31; §29 fines violations of §§16 to 27, and of orders and regulations made under them, $10 to $100. The University of Massachusetts Extension's manual (not official) says the Department cites c. 128, §2 and §§16 to 31A. Phase-outs (the list's asterisk): Chinese silver grass, Miscanthus sinensis, December 8, 2025 through December 31, 2026; jetbead, Rhodotypos scandens, December 8, 2025 through December 31, 2027; black alder, Alnus glutinosa, December 8, 2025 through December 31, 2028; sapphire berry, Symplocos paniculata, May 11, 2026 through May 11, 2028; Japanese angelica tree, Aralia elata, May 11, 2026 through May 11, 2029. Until each date the plant is listed (nurseries may sell existing stock); after it, it should move to the class prohibited (ban). The phase-out classes say "after" the last day of sale; the decisions don't restate the ban itself. Callery pear, Pyrus calleryana, is also asterisked: the list page's phase-out table gives September 19, 2024 as its deadline for import and propagation and December 31, 2028 for all sales, "with limited exceptions in orchards" (linked to the Department's September 2024 update, not read): listed until then, like the others. The table's dates for the other five agree with the decisions'. Permits and exceptions, each said in its own line (classes prohibitedPermit and prohibitedBonsai): water spinach, Ipomoea aquatica, is printed "[PERMIT REQUIRED – contact MDAR]"; Japanese black pine, Pinus thunbergii, "[Limited exceptions for bonsai growers, contact MDAR for details]". Water chestnut, Trapa natans, is on the list and also banned by statute (M.G.L. c. 128, §20A: "No person shall knowingly plant, transport, transplant or traffic in plants of water chestnut (Trapa natans) or in seeds or nuts thereof nor in any manner cause the spread or growth of such plants"; fine $10 to $100, §29): shown by the statute's class. Genus entries ("spp."): Aeginetia, Alectra and Striga. Cape tulip, printed "Homeria spp.; Moraea spp.", is not entered: Homeria is now part of Moraea, and Moraea read whole would take in every Moraea, garden species included; the federal list names the Cape tulips (Moraea collina, M. flaccida, M. miniata, M. ochroleuca, M. pallida). Left out: "Non-native Orobanche spp." and "Non-native Cuscuta spp.", since the list names neither the natives it spares nor the others (the federal list's genus entries, which except the natives by name, already cover the non-native broomrapes and dodders); Caulerpa taxifolia, an alga. Synonyms printed after a semicolon are recorded as other names ("also"), "ssp." written "subsp.": Egeria densa (Elodea densa, Anacharis densa); Digitaria abyssinica (D. scalarum); Frangula alnus (Rhamnus frangula); Mimosa diplotricha (M. invisa); Fallopia japonica (Polygonum cuspidatum, Reynoutria japonica); Salix atrocinerea (Salix cinerea ssp. oleifolia); Ficaria verna (Ranunculus ficaria); Monochoria vaginalis (Pontederia vaginalis); Centaurea biebersteinii (C. stoebe ssp. micranthos); Carthamus oxyacanthus (C. oxycantha). Misspellings: "Lycium ferrocissimum" (L. ferocissimum); "Setaria pallidifusca; S. pallidefusca; S. pumila" entered as the first, with the second as its spelling; S. pumila, yellow foxtail as a whole, is not added as another name (the common names printed are "cattail grass, yellow foxtail"; the federal list names the plant Setaria pumila subsp. pallidefusca); "Pennisetum polystachyon; P. polystachion" entered as the first, with the second as its spelling. Hybrids: Bell's honeysuckle is printed "Lonicera x bella [L. morrowii x L. tatarica]", entered as Lonicera × bella. Plume grass is printed "Miscanthus sacchariflorus (also covers Miscanthus x giganteus, a hybrid of M. sacchariflorus and M. sinensis)": the species is entered, and Miscanthus × giganteus too, since the list names it. Kudzu is printed Pueraria montana (check it matches the catalog's kudzu, Kew's Pueraria montana var. lobata). The list excepts no native forms: Phragmites australis includes the native subspecies americanus, and Phalaris arundinacea its native populations; black locust, Robinia pseudoacacia, variable water-milfoil, Myriophyllum heterophyllum, velvet mesquite, Prosopis velutina, and tornillo, Prosopis reptans, are native elsewhere in North America. Not read: 330 CMR 9.03, the currant and gooseberry (Ribes) quarantine (mass.gov). Left out: §24 (abatement of land overgrown with noxious weeds; it names no plants), the seed law (c. 128, §§84 to 101), and advisory lists, among them the Massachusetts Invasive Plant Advisory Group's. Reviewer (2026-10-31): the class sentences for phase-outs name the date after which the plant is prohibited. Read 2026-11-01 from the list page Jason saved (mass.gov refuses automated readers), a blind second reading agreeing: its statement of what the list forbids, and the phase-out table with Callery pear's dates. Kew's accepted names (2026-10-31), by which these are also matched: Pennisetum macrourum as Cenchrus caudatus; Egeria densa as Elodea densa; Eichhornia azurea as Pontederia azurea; Prosopis strombulifera as Strombocarpa strombulifera; Leptochloa chinensis as Dinebra chinensis; Cynanchum louiseae as Vincetoxicum nigrum; Emex spinosa as Rumex spinosus; Salvinia herzogii as Salvinia biloba; Humulus japonicus as Humulus scandens; Fallopia japonica as Reynoutria japonica; Prosopis pallida as Neltuma pallida; Pennisetum clandestinum as Cenchrus clandestinus; Pennisetum pedicellatum as Cenchrus pedicellatus; Ficaria verna as Ranunculus ficaria; Polygonum perfoliatum as Persicaria perfoliata; Monochoria hastata as Pontederia hastata; Cynanchum rossicum as Vincetoxicum rossicum; Monochoria vaginalis as Pontederia vaginalis; Senecio jacobaea as Jacobaea vulgaris; Emex australis as Rumex hypogaeus; Prosopis reptans as Strombocarpa reptans; Prosopis velutina as Neltuma velutina; Mycelis muralis as Lactuca muralis; Salsola vermiculata as Caroxylon vermiculatum. Matched only as printed (Kew gives no one accepted species for them, or a broader one): Setaria pallidifusca, Pennisetum polystachyon, Ampelopsis brevipedunculata, Centaurea biebersteinii.

jurisdictions.notes: Read 2026-11-01 from the Department of State's rules site (flrules.org: chapters 5B-57 and 5B-64, saved whole) and the Legislature's site (2026 Florida Statutes 581.091, 581.083, 369.25, 369.251). Effect of the noxious list: Rule 5B-57.004(1), "It is unlawful to introduce, multiply, possess, move, or release any arthropod, plant pest, biological control agent, noxious weed, or invasive plant regulated by the Department or the USDA except under permit issued by the Department", a permit being issued only where the Department finds the plant "can be contained to prevent escape into the environment"; and F.S. 581.091(1), "It is unlawful for any person to knowingly sell, offer for sale, or distribute any noxious weed". No permit is needed where possession "has resulted from natural dispersion and there is neither danger of nor intent to further disperse the plant", or to carry noxious or prohibited aquatic plants for disposal (5B-57.004(1)). Rule 5B-57.007(3): "the prohibited status also applies to any synonyms". The prohibited aquatic plants (Class II of Rule 5B-64.011, the same three as 5B-57.007(2)) may be possessed only under a permit (5B-64.003(2)), with the same natural-dispersion exemption (5B-64.010(6)); F.S. 369.25(2): "No person shall import, transport, cultivate, collect, sell, or possess any noxious aquatic plant listed on the prohibited aquatic plant list established by the department without a permit". Rule 5B-64.011(1) still prints a Class I list of 24 prohibited aquatic plants ("Under no circumstances will these species be permitted for possession, collection, transportation, cultivation, and importation except as provided in Rule 5B-64.004"); all 24 are also on the noxious list of 5B-57.007(1), so they are entered once, as noxious. F.S. 369.251(1) separately says "A person may not sell, transport, collect, cultivate, or possess any plant, including any part or seed, of the species Melaleuca quinquenervia, Schinus terebinthifolius, Casuarina equisetifolia, Casuarina glauca, or Mimosa pigra without a permit"; all five are on the noxious list. Permit exception: Casuarina cunninghamiana may be planted under special permit as a windbreak for commercial citrus groves in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie Counties, using male trees vegetatively propagated by permitted nurseries (F.S. 581.091(5); Rule 5B-57.012). The list prints Casuarina cunninghamiana, C. equisetifolia, C. glauca and "Casuarina spp.": each is entered. Chinese privet is printed "Ligustrum sinense – Chinese privet, except the cultivars ‘Variegatum’ and Sunshine’" (one quotation mark missing); it has its own class so the line states the exception. Dodders: "Cuscuta spp. Only the native Florida species are excluded from this list. These include:" eight species printed with the genus abbreviated ("C. americana" and so on), written out here as the exceptions; "These include" may not be a closed list. Broomrapes: "Orobanche spp. – broomrapes, with the exception of O. uniflora", written out. "Salvinia spp.(excluding S. minima – watermoss" is printed without its closing parenthesis. Misspelled as printed: "Carthamus oxyacantha" (Carthamus oxyacanthus), "Rubus molluccanus" (Rubus moluccanus), "Pennisetum polystachyon" (Pennisetum polystachion). "Rubus fruticosus – bramble blackberry" is listed: a garden blackberry filed under that name would be matched. In force: Rule 5B-57.007 was last amended effective September 28, 2020 (that amendment moved the Class I prohibited aquatic plants onto the noxious list). The rule's history on flrules.org shows later review-committee public meetings only (Pistia stratiotes, Ligustrum sinense 'Variegatum' and Vallisneria, November 19, 2024; Phyllanthus fluitans and Millettia pinnata, 2025; Nandina domestica, June 18, 2026), and no proposed or adopted amendment, so nothing from them is entered. Left out: Rule 5B-57.011 (a permit to cultivate any nonnative plant in plantings larger than two contiguous acres, F.S. 581.083(4); no permit is issued for a listed noxious weed), which names no plants but its exemptions; the industrial hemp rules 5B-57.013 and 5B-57.014, a licensing program for a crop; Rule 5B-40, Preservation of Native Flora of Florida, which protects native plants and was not read; the Division of Plant Industry's pest and disease quarantines (5B-3 and the citrus, lethal yellowing and other pest chapters), certification rules for host plants, not read beyond their titles; the seed law's noxious weed seed lists; and advisory lists (Florida Invasive Species Council, UF/IFAS assessments), which are not law.

jurisdictions.notes: Read 2026-11-01 from the Library of Maryland Regulations (regs.maryland.gov, where dsd.maryland.gov's COMAR pages now redirect), the General Assembly's statute pages and the Department of Agriculture's page holding the list. Invasive plants: since the 2024 law (Agriculture Article title 9.5) and the regulations adopted as an emergency effective January 15, 2026 and permanently effective July 20, 2026, Maryland has one class, the prohibited invasive plant (the old Tier 1 and Tier 2 and Tier 2's signs are gone: Regulation .07 repealed). COMAR 15.06.04.06A: "Prohibited invasive plants are those plants listed on the Consolidated List of Maryland Invasive Plant Species found on the Maryland Department of Agriculture's website, Plant Protection and Weed Management page"; the entries are from that page's table. Effect: Agriculture Article § 9.5-302(b)(1) and COMAR 15.06.04.04A, "a person may not propagate, import, transfer, sell, purchase, transport, or introduce any living part of a prohibited invasive plant in the State", except with the Secretary's prior approval for disposal, control, research or education, or export; a person who is not a commercial entity may control a plant on site, or take it off site for identification or disposal, without asking (15.06.04.04C). § 9.5-302(a): it does not apply to the sale of real property on which a prohibited plant grows. Phase-out (15.06.04.06B): a person in possession of a prohibited plant must comply within 1 year of its effective date on the list, or 2 years for a woody plant growing in the ground; "A person may not acquire a new prohibited invasive plant after that plant's effective date"; and "During the phase-out period, a person may only sell the existing stock of a prohibited invasive plant that person has in inventory as of the date the plant was placed on the prohibited invasive plant list"; licensed nurseries may ask for one more year. The list gives each plant's dates: effective 6/1/2024 with no phase-out (prohibited: the former Tier 1 plants, "classif[ied] as prohibited invasive plants" by § 9.5-301.1(a)); effective 1/15/2026, phase-out ending 1/15/2027 potted and 1/15/2028 in the ground; and effective 7/15/2026, ending 7/15/2027 and 7/15/2028. On 2026-11-01 the last two groups are in their phase-out, when existing stock may still be sold, so they are tiered listed; each becomes a ban when its phase-out ends (January 15, 2027 for potted stock of the January group). The page lists the July 2026 additions as "species and associated cultivars". Cultivars exempted ("List updated March 2, 2026"): Berberis thunbergii 'UCONNBTB048' Lemon Glow; Nandina domestica 'AKA' (Blush Pink), 'Firepower' and 'Lemon-Lime'; those two species have their own classes so the line states the exception. Names printed as alternatives each have an entry: "Berberis bealei / Mahonia bealei", "Cenchrus alopecuroides / Cenchrus purpurascens / Pennisetum alopecuroides". "Wisteria x formosa" ("floribunda x sinensis hybrid") is written with ×. The page's table is headed "List updated January 2026" though it includes the July 15, 2026 additions. Not on the page, so not entered: the Watch List, which a landscaper who plants or supplies a Watch List plant must give the customer (15.06.04.06E(3)), and which the Department is to post; and the "Next Plants To Be Assessed" (not law). Noxious weeds: COMAR 15.06.05.03 lists eight; Agriculture Article § 9-404(a): "No person may: (1) Import or transport a noxious weed in the State in any form capable of growth; or (2) Contaminate any uninfested land with a noxious weed through the movement of rootstocks, seed, soil, mulch, nursery stock, farm machinery, or any other artificial medium", and (b) landowners "shall eradicate or control the noxious weed". Misspelled as printed: "Sorghum biclor" (Sorghum bicolor), "Circium arvense" and "Circium vulgare" (Cirsium). Left out: "Shattercane (Sorghum biclor)", the weedy form of Sorghum bicolor: the species entry would take in grain and sweet sorghum and broomcorn (as Louisiana's sorghum line is read narrower). "Tall Waterhemp (Amaranthus tuberculatus, A. rudis)": both entered, abbreviation written out. Aquatic plants (Department of Natural Resources, COMAR 08.02.19.04): §A, "A person may not import, transport, purchase, possess, propagate, sell, or release into State waters" Salvinia molesta and Caulerpa taxifolia ("Green Caulerpa seaweed", an alga, entered as printed); §B, "A person may not transport" Egeria densa, Hydrilla verticillata, Myriophyllum aquaticum, Myriophyllum brasiliense and Trapa natans, where "Transport" means "to move a nonnative aquatic organism from the waters of one watershed ... and introduce it into the waters of another watershed" (.02B(13)); selling and growing them remain legal, so that class is listed. Permits: .04D. Left out: the stop-sale and treatment orders for weeds infesting nursery stock (COMAR 15.06.02.12, common names only: mugwort, Bermudagrass, dodder, Johnsongrass, poison ivy, thistles, witchweed, mile-a-minute, yellow nutsedge); the certificate rule for vegetable transplants (15.06.01); ginseng harvest (15.06.03); the Secretary's power to quarantine an exotic plant (§ 9-402(6)), under which no quarantine was found in COMAR 15.06; the seed law; and advisory lists (Maryland Invasive Species Council, Plant Invaders of Mid-Atlantic Natural Areas), which are not law. Left out: "Caulerpa taxifolia", an alga, as on the federal list.
