jurisdictions.notes: Read 2026-11-01 from the Revisor of Statutes (2026 Minnesota Statutes chapters 18 and 84D, Minnesota Rules chapter 6216) and the Department of Agriculture's list page. The noxious weed list is not in a rule: Minn. Stat. 18.79, subd. 13, has the commissioner "prepare, publish, and revise as necessary, but at least once every three years, a list of noxious weeds and their designated classification"; the Department's page calls itself "the official Minnesota Noxious Weed List" and says "All listed species on the Minnesota noxious weed list include all hybrids, cultivars, and varieties unless specifically exempted." Effects, Minn. Stat. 18.771: (b) "Prohibited-eradicate noxious weeds may not be sold or propagated in Minnesota" and must be eradicated; (c) "Prohibited-control noxious weeds may not be propagated or sold in Minnesota" and must be controlled; both: "Transportation of the propagating parts ... is prohibited except as allowed under section 18.82"; (d) restricted noxious weeds "and their propagating parts ... may not be imported, sold, or transported in the state, except as allowed by permit under section 18.82"; (e) specially regulated plants have "Species-specific management plans or rules that define the use and management requirements", given in the list's "Special regulation" column. 18.82 permits are for transport along public roads, disposal, and possession for research or education. Plants added in January 2026 (stiltgrass, autumn olive, creeping meadow foxtail and the three phase-out plants) are in force. Japanese barberry: "only the cultivars listed below are prohibited from sale"; the list names 24 cultivars, "B. thunbergii var. atropurpurea" and "Wild Type (parent species – green barberry)"; "All other Japanese barberry cultivars not listed above are in a three-year production phase out period and may be sold through December 31, 2028. Beginning January 1, 2029, all non-exempt cultivars will be classified as Restricted Noxious Weeds"; exempt: ‘UCONNBTCP4N’ Crimson Cutie, ‘UCONNBTB039’ Mr. Green Genes, ‘UCONNBTB048’ Lemon Glow, ‘UCONNBTB113’ Lemon Cutie and ‘NCBT1’ Mini Maroon. The species entry takes in every cultivar, so the class is a ban whose line states the cultivars still for sale. 'Bailsel' and 'Tara' are printed as "B. koreana × B. thunbergii hybrid". Glossy buckthorn is listed "(and all cultivars)", Norway maple "(and all cultivars)". Siberian peashrub: "exemption for Green Spires® Caragana - Caragana 'Jefarb'"; winged burning bush: "exemption for ZeroSeed’: ZeroSeed Blaze TM and Proven Winners ® ‘NCEA1’: Fire Ball Seedless TM" (printed so). Amur corktree: "Only sales of named male cultivars are permitted. Sales of all other Phellodendron amurense are prohibited." Amur, Norway and Tatarian maples may be sold with the label the list quotes; the class is listed. Common butterbur, giant butterbur and rowan mountain ash: "Three-year production phase-out period after the sale of this species will be prohibited, and the species will be designated as Restricted in 2029"; sale is still legal on 2026-11-01, so the class is listed until then. Left out: "Pastinaca sativa L. (except for non-wild cultivated varieties)" (wild parsnip), which no species name can tell from the garden parsnip; county noxious weeds, which each county designates and enforces; and poison ivy, delisted in 2025. The page also says "Federal terrestrial and parasitic listed noxious weeds are prohibited in Minnesota": not a designation in any category, so not entered (the federal list has its own entry). Misspelled as printed: "Polygonum sachalinese" (Polygonum sachalinense), "Miscanthus saccariflorus" (Miscanthus sacchariflorus). "Euphorbia virgata ... and E. esula" are two entries; "ssp." is written "subsp." and "x" as "×". Left out: "Wild carrot/Queen Anne's Lace, Daucus carota L." (restricted): the list's rule takes in all varieties unless exempted, so the species entry would take in the garden carrot (as Michigan's wild carrot is left out). Black locust (Robinia pseudoacacia) is restricted. Aquatic plants (Department of Natural Resources): Minn. Stat. 84D.05, subd. 1, "A person may not possess, import, purchase, sell, propagate, transport, or introduce a prohibited invasive species", except under a permit and other listed exceptions; part 6216.0250, subp. 1, designates the species "and any hybrids, cultivars, or varieties of the species"; Eurasian watermilfoil "including its hybrids"; purple loosestrife "(Lythrum salicaria, Lythrum virgatum, or any variety, hybrid, or cultivar thereof)"; common reed "nonnative subspecies (Phragmites australis ssp. australis, not including Phragmites australis ssp. americanus)". Starry stonewort (Nitellopsis obtusa) and Caulerpa taxifolia are algae, entered as printed. Subpart 2a: "Aquatic plants listed in Code of Federal Regulations, title 7, section 360.200, are designated as prohibited invasive species, except for Chinese water spinach (Ipomoea aquatica)"; entered here from the federal list's "(a) Aquatic and wetland weeds" (7 CFR 360.200, January 1, 2025 edition, saved as us-360-2025): the 14 not already named in subpart 2 (the federal list prints Caulerpa taxifolia as the "Mediterranean strain"). Regulated invasive species (part 6216.0260): Minn. Stat. 84D.07, "a person may not introduce a regulated invasive species without a permit"; "introduction" means "the placement, release, or escape of a nonnative species into a free-living state" (84D.01, subd. 9), and a water garden with no outlet to public waters is not a free-living state (6216.0200, subp. 3a); selling and growing them remain legal, so the class is listed. Nonnative waterlilies: "nonnative waterlilies (Nymphaea spp.) Linnaeus, or any variety, hybrid, or cultivar thereof. Native Minnesota waterlilies are: Nymphaea odorata Aiton subsp. odorata Aiton, N. leibergii Morong, and N. odorata Aiton subsp. tuberosa": entered as the genus except Nymphaea odorata (both its subspecies native) and N. leibergii. Not read: the plant pest quarantines (Minn. Stat. chapter 18G and its rules) and the nursery law (chapter 18H). Left out: Minn. Stat. 84D.09, which bars transporting aquatic macrophytes in general (not a list); the seed law's noxious weed seed lists; and advisory lists, which are not law. Left out: "Caulerpa taxifolia" and "Nitellopsis obtusa", algae, as on the federal list.

jurisdictions.notes: Read 2026-11-01. The rules are the official PDFs from the Secretary of State's Code of Colorado Regulations; the statutes are the Office of Legislative Legal Services' 2024 printout of title 35 (the 2025 printout was not at the same address, and searches found no 2025 or 2026 act amending sections 35-5.5-104.5, 35-5.5-108 or 35-26-105). Effect of all three noxious weed lists: C.R.S. 35-5.5-104.5(1)(a), "It shall be unlawful to intentionally introduce, cultivate, sell, offer for sale, or knowingly allow to grow in violation of this article or any rule promulgated hereunder in this state any noxious weed designated pursuant to section 35-5.5-108 (2)(a)", except sanctioned research, activities the commissioner permits, and approved reclamation plans; (1)(b) "It shall not be a violation of this section for a person to knowingly allow to grow a state noxious weed that is being properly managed". Section 35-5.5-108(2)(a) is the section that creates List A, List B and List C, so the sale ban covers all three; the Department's 2023 statement for adding Siberian elm and tree of heaven to List C says it was done "to prevent future sale of these species". Lists, as 35-5.5-108(2)(a) defines them: List A "rare noxious weed species that are subject to eradication wherever detected statewide"; List B "subject to eradication, containment, or suppression in portions of the state designated by the commissioner"; List C "widespread and well-established noxious weed species for which control is recommended but not required by the state, although local governing bodies may require management". The Watch List was removed from the rules in 2020 and is not entered. Nursery rule: C.R.S. 35-26-105(1), "A person shall not sell, offer for sale, or distribute: ... (c) Noxious weeds or nursery stock that is infested with noxious weeds", where a "noxious weed" is one "the commissioner has identified as a prohibited weed by rule" (35-26-102(11.6)); 8 CCR 1203-5, Part 9.0: "The following plant species shall not be sold as nursery stock within the State of Colorado or contaminate nursery stock". That list (last amended 2019) is older than the noxious weed lists: it still names plants since taken off them (Anoda cristata and Hibiscus trionum, removed from List B in 2014; Lespedeza cuneata; Tamarix parviflora, removed from List B in 2020) and plants never on them (Anthemis arvensis, Lythrum virgatum), and it uses older names (Alhagi pseudalhagi, Cardaria draba, Acroptilon repens, Centaurea maculosa, Centaurea pratensis for meadow knapweed, Chrysanthemum leucanthemum, Matricaria perforata, Elytrigia repens, Polygonum cuspidatum, Polygonum sachalinense, Polygonum x bohemicum); all its names are entered as printed, in their own class, so a plant on both lists has two entries. It prints "Black henbane (Hyoscyamus niger)" twice (entered once), "Bohemiam knotweed", and some names with wrong capitals, written here as names: "Anthemis Arvensis", "Dipsacus Laciniatus", "brassica elongata", "polygonum sachalinense", "hibiscus trionum"; "L. genistifolia" and the second names of "Lythrum salicaria and L. virgatum", "Tamarix parviflora and T. ramosissima" and "Onopordum acanthium and O. tauricum" are written out. In the noxious weed lists: "Salt cedar (Tamarix chinensis and T. ramosissima)" is two entries; "ssp." is written "subsp." (Centaurea stoebe subsp. micranthos), and "x" as "×" (Fallopia × bohemicum, Centaurea × moncktonii, Centaurea × psammogena). Misspelled as printed: "Fallopia sachalinense" (Fallopia sachalinensis); "Fallopia x bohemicum" is Fallopia × bohemica. Left out: "Yellow x Dalmatian toadflax hybrid (Linaria vulgaris x L. dalmatica)", a hybrid written by its parents. The lists name "Wild caraway (Carum carvi)" (List B), "Wild proso millet (Panicum miliaceum)" and "Chicory (Cichorium intybus)" (List C), and the species entries take in culinary caraway, proso millet and chicory, radicchio and witloof. They are kept, unlike Michigan's wild carrot: the nursery rule (Part 9.0) names all three as species that "shall not be sold as nursery stock". Also listed: oxeye daisy, dame's rocket, bouncingbet, St. Johnswort, absinth wormwood and yellow nutsedge (chufa). In force: 8 CCR 1206-2 was last amended effective May 15, 2025 (ventenata added to List A); 8 CCR 1203-5 effective October 30, 2019. Not read beyond their titles: the Department's pest quarantines (8 CCR 1203-13 late blight, 1203-18 Prunus into the San Luis Valley, 1203-21 Japanese beetle, 1203-24 emerald ash borer), certification rules for host plants; left out: county and municipal noxious weed lists (C.R.S. 35-5.5-108(3)), the seed act's noxious weed seeds (8 CCR 1203-6), and advisory lists. The Department of Agriculture's own site (ag.colorado.gov) refused automated readers (HTTP 403 from its CloudFront), so nothing there was read.

jurisdictions.notes: Read 2026-11-01 from the Washington State Legislature's WAC and RCW pages, with the two Washington State Register filings that last changed the quarantine list. Quarantine: WAC 16-752-620, "It is prohibited to transport, buy, sell, offer for sale, or to distribute plants or plant parts of the regulated species listed in WAC 16-752-610 into or within the state of Washington or to sell, offer for sale, or distribute seed packets of the seed, flower seed blends, or wildflower mixes of these regulated species into or within the state of Washington"; the quarantine area is every county of the state and all other states (16-752-605); 16-752-610: "Regulated status also applies to all synonyms of these botanical names and interspecies hybrids if both parents are regulated species"; 16-752-630 excepts herbarium, research, educational and disposal uses, and 16-752-640 lets the director allow prohibited activities "by compliance agreement". English ivy (Hedera helix) and Atlantic ivy (Hedera hibernica) are quarantined as whole species since WSR 25-15-040 (effective August 9, 2025), which added them with 17 other species "which would prohibit their sale and distribution"; no phase-in is given. Class C of the noxious weed list still names "English ivy 4 cultivars only: Hedera hibernica 'Hibernica', Hedera helix 'Baltica', Hedera helix 'Pittsburgh', Hedera helix 'Star'"; these cultivars are left out of Class C, since a species entry would take in every ivy, and the quarantine entries cover them. Kept with a line of their own, the exceptions named: "Arundo donax (except variegated cultivars)", "Buddleia davidii (except accepted sterile cultivars)" (the rule does not say who accepts them) and "Foeniculum vulgare (except bulbing fennel, F. vulgare var. azoricum)", which the rule names for sale and which takes in herb and bronze fennel; the same fennel is Class B, with the same exception. Left out: "Daucus carota (except for subsp. sativus)" (quarantine) and "wild carrot (except subs. sativus where grown commercially or for food)" (Class C), since a species entry would take in the garden carrot the rule excepts. jurisdictions.notes: Read 2026-11-01 from the Secretary of State's Oregon Administrative Rules Database (division 52 of chapter 603, in full) and the Legislature's 2025 edition of ORS chapters 561 and 569. OAR 603-052-1200(7): "(a) All plants covered in section (3) of this rule are prohibited entry into the State of Oregon. (b) All plants listed in section (3) of this rule are prohibited from transport, purchase, sale or offering for sale in the State of Oregon. (c) All plants listed in section (3) of this rule are prohibited from being propagated in the State of Oregon"; (d) they "may be collected from the wild in areas that are already infested", but not for propagation or sale. Section (3): "the term 'plants' applies to whole plants, plant parts, and seeds", and the rule covers all "A" and "B" weeds and the federal list: "Plants on the Federal Noxious Weed List (7 C.F.R. 360.200) are also covered by this rule, with the exception of Japanese blood grass, Imperata cylindrica, var. Red Baron and Chinese water spinach, Ipomoea aquatica." Section (9): the director "may issue a permit allowing entry into this state, propagation, or research", for at most a year. Section (6) exempts agricultural seed (subject to the seed law's tolerances) and commodities "to the extent that they are contaminated with noxious weed seed". "A" weeds must also be reported within 48 hours and controlled (4)(c), (f); for "B" weeds the goal is "control and prevention of new infestations" (5)(b). Butterfly bush is listed "Buddleja davidii (B. variabilis)*", with the note: "Plants being sold in Oregon that are labeled 'Butterfly Bush' are assumed to be B. davidii and will be subject to a stop sale order. ODA approved sterile varieties of Buddleja that produce less than 2% viable seed and inter-specific hybrids that are not regulated, and may be propagated and sold if labeled with the approved variety name"; it has a line of its own. English ivy and Atlantic ivy are listed as whole species. Common reed is printed as the whole species, "Phragmities australis", the native subspecies too. Ribbongrass is "Phalaris arundinacea var. Picta", the variety only (written var. picta); reed canarygrass is not listed. Written as names: "Fallopia x bohemica" as Fallopia × bohemica; "Hieracium floribundum" (yellow hawkweed) as Hieracium × floribundum; "Yellowtuft — Alyssum murale, A. corsicum" as two entries; "Large-flower — Ludwigia grandiflora ssp." as the species, since no subspecies is named. Misspelled as printed: "Sagittaria platyphyla", "Phragmities australis", "Orabanche minor". Synonyms printed in parentheses are not entered: "(R. procerus, R. discolor)", "(B. variabilis)", "(C. maculosa)", "(Polygonum)", "(Elodea)". The rule also takes in the federal list by reference, except Japanese blood grass (only the variety 'Red Baron') and water spinach (Ipomoea aquatica). It isn't adopted here as a class of Oregon's: the federal list's own line already shows in every state, and an adopted class can't name Oregon's two exceptions, so it would show them as banned by Oregon. Left out: the Department's pest quarantines on host plants (grape, chestnut and chinquapin, elm, peach, plum, hops, hazelnut nursery stock, blueberry, Phytophthora ramorum hosts, Allium leafminer hosts and others in division 52), which set conditions for bringing plants in from infested areas or for named control areas and ban no plant statewide; the small broomrape quarantine (OAR 603-052-1025), which governs clover seed and is covered by small broomrape's own "B" listing; the moss ball rule (OAR 603-052-1391), an alga with zebra mussels; the seed law's noxious weed seed tolerances (OAR 603-056-0205); county lists; and advisory lists.

Prohibited genera: IDAPA 02.06.09.220.01.a, "All plants and plant parts in the genera of: Cytisus, Genista, Spartium, and Chamaecytisus additionally including 'all' subtaxa of these plant genera are prohibited in Idaho"; the rule says no more of what "prohibited" forbids. Each genus is entered whole: every broom, including the garden Genista and Cytisus species and hybrids. Invasive plants: Idaho Code 22-1905, "No person may import, export, purchase, sell, barter, distribute, propagate, transport or introduce an invasive species into or within the state of Idaho and no person may possess an invasive species", except under a permit, for identification or disposal, or as dead or preserved specimens; IDAPA 02.06.09.120 adds "possess, cultivate" and "Releasing, placing, planting". The rule lists invasive plants as energy crops (149: "Arundo donax (and hybrids)", "Pueraria montana (and hybrids)", "Chinese Silver Grass — Miscanthus giganteus (and hybrids)", "Jatropha curcus (and hybrids)", "Cold Tolerant Eucalyptis (and hybrids)") and trap crops (150: "Solanum sisymbriifolium (and hybrids)", "Solanum nigrus (and hybrids)"), each with its own permit (124, 125); the species are entered, "and hybrids" is not. "Miscanthus giganteus" is the giant miscanthus hybrid, written Miscanthus × giganteus (the common name printed with it, Chinese silver grass, is usually M. sinensis's, which is not listed). Left out: "Cold Tolerant Eucalyptis", which names no species. Noxious weeds: Idaho Code 22-2407(1), "It shall be the duty and responsibility of all landowners to control noxious weeds on their land and property"; EDRR weeds "shall be reported to the Department within ten (10) days following positive identification" and "shall be eradicated during the same growing season as identified" (220.02); Control and Prohibited Genera weeds need a control authority's written plan "to reduce known populations in not more than five (5) years" (220.01.b, 220.03). IDAPA 02.06.09.230.02: "No article containing noxious weed propagules shall be sold or furnished to any person within this state, until it has been treated in a manner sufficient to eliminate all noxious weed propagating capability", and 220.05.e names "Nursery stock including plant material propagated for the support of aquarium, pet, or horticultural activities" among such articles; the rule does not say this bars selling a noxious weed itself as nursery stock, so the three lists are listed, as Arkansas's nursery-stock rule is. Written as names: "Polygonum X bohemicum" as Polygonum × bohemicum; "Linaria dalmatica ssp. dalmatica" as subsp.; "Tamarix spp." as the genus; "Myriophyllum spicatum (and hybrids)" as the species. Misspelled as printed: "Nymphoides pelata", "Iris pseudocorus", "Jatropha curcus", "Solanum nigrus", and "Centaurea triumfetti", printed for squarrose knapweed (Kew spells it triumfettii, a species of its own; squarrose knapweed is usually C. virgata). Left out: "Starry Stonewort — Nitellopsis obtusa" (EDRR), an alga; the weed-free forage program and its NAISMA list (Subchapter C), a voluntary certification; county noxious weeds, which "are not subject to provisions of the state noxious weed laws" (Idaho Code 22-2406(1)(k)); seed law; advisory lists; the invasive animals of sections 130 to 147.

Effects: R68-9-4(2), "Any person, company, or corporation may not sell, barter, or give away any noxious weed plants or seeds for any purpose", which covers all five classes; R68-9-3(6), Class 4 weeds are "Prohibited for sale or propagation", "a threat to the state through retail sales or propagation in the nursery and greenhouse industry"; R68-9-6(2), each county's general notice includes "a requirement that property owners control and prevent the spread of noxious weeds on land in their possession, or under their control", and an owner who does not act on a county's notice "is maintaining a public nuisance" (Utah Code 4-17-109(3)). Counties "may reprioritize these weeds for the county weed list" (R68-9-3(7)). Bermudagrass has a line of its own: R68-9-3(5)(v), "The department does not consider Bermudagrass as a noxious and invasive weed in Washington County"; (vi), "Triploid hybrid Bermudagrass purchased from a producer certified with the Utah Crop Improvement Association and the Nursery Inspection program is allowed for commercial and private uses throughout Utah." Read narrower than printed: "Field bindweed (Wild Morning-glory) — Convolvulus spp." as field bindweed, Convolvulus arvensis, which its common name names (read whole, the genus would take in the garden Convolvulus); "Perennial Sorghum spp. Including: Johnson grass Sorghum halepense, Columbus grass Sorghum almum" as those two (Sorghum almum written Sorghum × almum). "Phragmites (Common reed) — Phragmites australis ssp." names no subspecies and is entered as the species, though Class 3 weeds are declared "not native to Utah" and the native subspecies is not excepted by name. Hoary cress is entered by the rule's names (Lepidium draba, L. chalepense, L. appelianum), not the Cardaria names printed with them. Misspelled as printed: "Brassicas elongate", "Alliaria petiolate", "Cynoglossum officianale"; "Myriophyllum spicatum L." is entered without its author. Left out: prohibited and restricted noxious weed seeds (R68-8-2), a seed-law list; county noxious weeds; advisory lists.

jurisdictions.notes: Read 2026-11-02. Both quarantines are scanned, signed orders of the Director of the Division of Agriculture as State Plant Quarantine Officer; their text was read from the page images (the saved .txt copies are OCR). Their authority: 11 AAC 34.130(a), "The director may establish, maintain and enforce such quarantine regulations as he deems necessary to protect the agricultural industry of this state from pests, by establishing quarantine at the boundaries of this state or elsewhere within the state"; AS 03.05.010(b)(2), the commissioner may issue "orders, regulations, quarantines, and embargoes relating to ... establishment of quarantines for eradication of pests"; and AS 03.05.090(a), a person who violates "a regulation, order, or quarantine made under authority of this chapter ... is guilty of a class A misdemeanor". Aquatic weeds (2014): "It is prohibited to import, transport, buy, sell, offer for sale, or distribute plants or plant parts of the regulated species within the state of Alaska. It is further prohibited to intentionally transplant wild plants and/or plant parts of these species within the state of Alaska." It has no permit clause (the Division's aquatic invasives page says intentional movement other than for identification "must be permitted through the Division of Agriculture"). Printed "Elodea Canadensis", entered lower-case. Prunus (2025), "to prevent the entry and movement within the State": "It is prohibited to import, transport, buy, sell, offer for sale, or distribute whole or parts of these restricted species within the State of Alaska. It is further prohibited to intentionally transplant wild plants and/or plant parts of these species within the State of Alaska without written consent of the Director." Materials regulated: "All whole plants, and all propagule parts of regulated plants." It names the species only: no cultivar is excepted (chokecherry cultivars such as 'Canada Red' are taken in), and it says nothing of trees already growing. Both say "Regulated status also applies to all synonyms" of the names. Left out: Alaska's noxious weed list, 11 AAC 34.020 (14 prohibited and 9 restricted noxious weeds), a seed-law list. It sits in 11 AAC 34, Article 1 (Seed Regulations), and every rule that applies it concerns seed: 34.075(a)(3)-(4) and (f) forbid selling, transporting or planting seed that contains prohibited noxious weed seed, or restricted noxious weed seed over its tolerance; (g) forbids using or selling screenings that contain them; 34.077 has shipments "infested with the seed of any prohibited noxious weed" returned. Nothing in 11 AAC 34 forbids selling, planting or growing the plants themselves. Also left out: the Exterior Quarantine of Aquatic Pests (April 2021), whose only plants are marimo or Cladophora balls (Aegagropila linnaei), an alga, beside clams, mussels and a snail; the seed-potato and potato late blight quarantines, pest quarantines on host plants; the Division's clarification sheet on the aquatic quarantine (guidance). Not read: Alaska Department of Fish and Game rules on releasing plants into state waters.

jurisdictions.notes: Read 2026-11-02 from the General Assembly's statutes pages (the site sends an incomplete certificate chain; fetched with the GoDaddy intermediate added, verification on). Section 22a-381d(a) to (c): "no person shall import, move, sell, purchase, transplant, cultivate or distribute any of the following invasive plants", and the same for "any reproductive portion" of them ("seeds, flowers, roots and tubers"); (d) excepts "the moving for eradication, research or educational purposes" and "the cultivating for research purposes"; (f) "fined not more than one hundred dollars per plant"; (e) no municipality may adopt an ordinance on the retail sale or purchase of any invasive plant. The class prohibited holds subsection (a)'s 62 plants (star of Bethlehem added by P.A. 25-126) and (b)(1) (from October 1, 2005) and (b)(2) (from October 1, 2024), all in force. Phase-in, future: (b)(3) callery pear, Pyrus calleryana, from October 1, 2027; (b)(4) from October 1, 2028: Frangula alnus, Rhamnus cathartica, Phalaris arundinacea, Euonymus alatus, Ligustrum vulgare, Robinia pseudoacacia, Miscanthus sinensis, Berberis thunbergii; (b)(5) Norway maple, Acer platanoides, from October 1, 2030. Until each date they are listed, not banned; from it their class should become prohibited, tier ban. "European buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica)" in (b)(4) is the same species as "common buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica)" in (a), already prohibited: entered once, under (a). Watercress, Rorippa nasturtium-aquaticum, is a crop the law names itself, "except for watercress sold for human consumption without its reproductive structure": kept, in a class that says so. Read as printed: "Lonicera xbella" as Lonicera × bella; "Phragmites australis" is the whole species, the native subspecies not excepted; Amorpha fruticosa, Froelichia gracilis, Nelumbo lutea, Silphium perfoliatum and Robinia pseudoacacia are named as species, with no exception for native stock. Misspelled as printed: "Eleagnus angustifolia", "Impatiens glanulifera", "Aegopodium podagraia". No sterile-cultivar exception: P.A. 26-129, § 1, only orders the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station to report by January 15, 2027 "on the safety of the use and planting, import, transport, sale and purchase of sterile cultivars and the distribution of Japanese barberry". Running bamboo, § 22a-381e: "any bamboo in the genus Phyllostachys, including Phyllostachys aureosulcata"; "No person shall plant running bamboo or allow running bamboo to be planted on his or her property at a location that is forty feet or less from any abutting property or public right-of-way" (fine $100, each day a separate offense); growing beyond the property is a nuisance and the owner is liable for damage and removal; each retail seller or installer must give a disclosure statement. Selling and growing it remain legal: listed. Left out: the Invasive Plants Council's list of invasive and potentially invasive plants (§§ 22a-381a, 22a-381b), which binds only state agencies' purchases (§ 22a-381c) and is otherwise advisory; the Agricultural Experiment Station's pest quarantines (Asian longhorned beetle, emerald ash borer, spotted lanternfly), which regulate host plants as carriers of a pest. No 2026 act other than P.A. 26-129 touching these sections was found; the 2027 Supplement is not yet published.
